analysis.one_liner: Bars federal and state regulators from setting broadband internet rates, terms, or quality rules.
analysis.headline: The broadband deregulation bill, introduced with no cosponsors, died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strip the Federal Communications Commission and every state government of the power to regulate the prices, terms, or conditions that broadband providers charge home internet customers. It would also free cable and telephone companies from any duty to share their broadband lines with independent internet providers, exempt new fiber lines from rules requiring phone companies to lease parts of their networks to competitors, and cap the fees cities can charge for letting providers dig up public streets. It would have replaced state consumer protections with a federal study that could take years, added accessibility requirements for people with disabilities, and raised the fines the FCC can impose on rule-breakers.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable companies and incumbent telephone companies offering home broadband. They would be free of rate and terms regulation, would no longer have to open their lines to independent internet providers, would keep their new fiber lines to themselves, and would pay cities no more than the direct cost of using public rights-of-way. Equipment makers would face new accessibility rules, but the bill's core transfers regulatory power away from the public and to the largest network owners.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids the FCC or any state from regulating the rates, charges, terms, or conditions of retail home broadband service, leaving prices entirely to the market [S2][S3].

It removes any federal or state requirement that a broadband provider give independent internet service providers access to its facilities, with only a temporary exception for obligations that already existed, and that exception expires after five years unless the FCC finds it necessary for competition [S2][S3].

It exempts new fiber loops and fiber feeder lines from the requirement that incumbent phone companies share network elements with competitors, and it frees them from collocation duties at remote terminals [S3].
It bars any state or local law that would impede an entity from offering broadband, and caps what cities can charge providers for use of public rights-of-way at direct actual costs [S2][S3].
Sponsor McCain's stated purpose was to let market forces drive investment and innovation in broadband for the benefit of all Americans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Home broadband customers, who would lose price and service-quality protections until and unless the FCC completed a study and issued new national rules years later; independent internet service providers, who would lose guaranteed access to the networks they need to reach customers; and cities and towns, which would lose rights-of-way revenue above bare administrative costs and much of their authority over local network builds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Broadband customers, independent ISPs, local governments

drawbacks.text: Under the bill, no state could regulate broadband service quality unless the FCC first spent up to two years studying the question and then chose to issue national rules, which could not take effect until at least two years after enactment; until then, consumers would have no quality regulation at all [S3].

By lifting the duty to share facilities with independent ISPs and exempting fiber from unbundling, the bill would let the dominant cable and phone companies control both the network and the retail service on it, squeezing out the competitors that had grown under the 1996 Telecom Act [S3].

Capping rights-of-way fees at direct administrative costs would cut revenue local governments use to manage street work and would make it harder for communities to recover the real costs of network construction in their rights-of-way [S3].

The strongest good-faith case for the bill was that heavy regulation discouraged investment in faster networks; an honest supporter would have to acknowledge the trade-off that consumers were asked to give up price and quality oversight on the promise of future investment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's consumer-facing pieces—disability access requirements for equipment and services, higher FCC fines up to $1 million per violation, and a rural broadband clearinghouse—are real but minor beside its centerpiece: a wholesale removal of federal, state, and local authority over the dominant providers of home internet. Consumers were being asked to surrender price, quality, and competition protections on the theory that market forces would replace them, with no backstop if they did not. The design heavily favored incumbent network owners.

outcome.mechanism: McCain introduced the bill in August 2002 and the Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee, which never acted on it; it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on August 1, 2002, near the end of the congressional session, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
The committee took no further action—no hearings, no markup, no floor vote—and the bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband customers and independent internet providers were better off, because the rate, quality, and open-network protections the bill would have repealed stayed on the books. Incumbent cable and phone companies gained nothing from the bill's death, though the fight over broadband deregulation continued in other forums.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ), sponsor; ranking member of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on August 1, 2002; no colleagues joined him as cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ernest Hollings (D-SC)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out; no hearing or markup was held before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it never reached a vote, so no party split can be measured; the Democratic-chaired committee to which it was referred took no action.

industries.note: The bill would free cable companies from any rate or terms regulation and from any requirement to open their networks to independent ISPs, while their main rivals lose guaranteed access to phone-company facilities. Customers would bear the cost of unregulated monopoly pricing and quality.

The bill exempts new fiber loops from the 1996 Telecom Act's unbundling and collocation duties and lifts retail price oversight, letting incumbent phone companies keep their newest networks to themselves while their competitors lose access. Consumers lose the competition that open access was designed to create.

These were the competitors—often small companies—whose business depended on being able to lease capacity on the big networks. The bill would remove that access, so their interest ran with ordinary customers who benefit from competition.

The bill would bar state or local rules that impede broadband providers and would cap rights-of-way fees at direct administrative costs, cutting revenue and local control over public streets. Communities lost negotiating power if the bill had passed.

The bill would require accessible design for people with disabilities unless that is an undue burden, adding compliance costs, but a national standard could simplify design across platforms. The burden on the industry is modest and the benefit goes to disabled users.
